realStack: Annual operating / strategic planning process (long-range plan, headcount and hiring-target plans)
Budget and financial models — discretionary-spend tracking, opex/headcount forecasting (spreadsheet/Excel-grade financial modeling, likely a corporate FP&A/EPM tool)
Executive communication artifacts — QBR decks, business cases, board/leadership presentations (PowerPoint/Google Slides-grade)
Org-design materials — org charts, capability maps, reorg / change-management plans for the Experience org (design, technical writing, research, program management)

Operating-cadence and program-management instruments — OKR/strategy frameworks, governance calendars, status/portfolio tracking (ServiceNow's own Strategic Portfolio Management / project tooling is the plausible internal system)
M&A / acquihire inputs — diligence summaries, integration and org-impact plans
Data-analysis tooling for synthesizing disparate operational data into recommendations (spreadsheets/BI dashboards)
NOTE: the JD names no specific software; this stack is inferred from the responsibilities, as is normal for a strategic-ops/chief-of-staff role
coreResponsibilities: Run the operating cadence for the Experience org (product/org strategy reviews, governance, change management) to keep the org healthy
Own annual planning and ongoing budget/change management in partnership with business units; manage overall budget, hiring targets, and discretionary spend
Spearhead complex cross-functional initiatives to build the future-state org structure and new capabilities, with actionable insights
Enable executive-level engagement — build business cases, QBRs, and communications that align Experience leaders with the broader ServiceNow business
Stand up and scale the strategic-operations function across design, documentation, and research disciplines
Participate in M&A activity (acquihires, tech-based acquisitions) where it affects org work and structure
Drive personnel/org change-management procedures including reorgs, and partner with peer leaders on best practices, inclusion, and skills development
statedVsRealGaps: Title vs. reality: 'Staff Strategic Operations Manager' reads as strategy, but the day-to-day (cadence, budget, change management, QBRs, reorgs) is a chief-of-staff / business-operations role for a creative org — source against COO-of-org/BizOps profiles, not pure case-team strategy

Management scope is ambiguous: 'Staff' at ServiceNow typically signals a senior individual contributor, yet the JD says 'leader,' 'talent management,' and 'manage hiring targets' — unclear whether the role has direct reports or leads purely through influence; this materially changes the hiring bar
The required years of experience are redacted/blank in the posting, so the precise seniority bar can't be read from the text — must be confirmed with the hiring team

Stated pedigree is 'strategy consulting / PE / product strategy,' but the actual work rewards operational rigor (financial planning, program governance, change execution); a classic strategy-consultant hire may be strong on framing yet thin on the recurring operational grind the role mostly is
M&A / acquihire involvement is listed almost in passing but is a high-stakes, specialized responsibility — its true weight and decision authority are underspecified
No tools or systems are named, so candidate evaluation has to lean on artifacts (models, decks, operating mechanisms they've built) rather than a stated toolset
riskAreas: Breadth-vs-depth mis-hire: the mandate spans strategy + FP&A/budget + program governance + change management + M&A + org design; very few candidates are genuinely strong across all, so one critical area (often financial rigor or M&A) tends to be weak
Level/title mismatch: 'Staff…Manager' invites confusion about people-management; a candidate expecting (or wanting to avoid) direct reports could be mismatched to the actual structure

Influence-without-authority dependency: success hinges on aligning a cross-functional creative org (designers, writers, researchers, PMs) the role may not manage — high organizational/political risk if the person lacks executive presence or partnering instinct

'Roll up your sleeves' alongside executive-level strategic influence signals an under-resourced or newly-forming function — risk of overload and unclear remit, especially since the role is also expected to *stand up* the strategic-ops arm itself
Redacted experience requirement creates calibration risk — easy to over- or under-level the hire without confirming the intended bar
Ambiguity tolerance is explicitly required; a structured-environment operator who needs defined process will likely struggle
analysis.reflection: This is a strong, content-rich JD for what is, in substance, a chief-of-staff / business-operations leader embedded in ServiceNow's Experience (design/research/writing/PM) organization — not the pure-strategy role the 'Strategic Operations' label and 'strategy consulting' qualification suggest. The real body of work is operational: running the org's planning and budget cadence, manufacturing executive-grade decision artifacts (QBRs, business cases, budgets), and executing org change — with episodic, high-stakes M&A involvement layered on top. The stated need (consulting pedigree, analytics, problem framing) is well aligned to the *thinking* the role demands, but diverges from the *doing*: the job is mostly recurring operational stewardship and cross-functional influence, where financial discipline and program execution matter as much as slide-ready strategy. The two evaluable risks a hiring team should pin down before sourcing are (1) the management/level ambiguity inherent in a 'Staff…Manager' title with redacted experience years, and (2) the very wide functional surface, which makes a balanced operator rare and a lopsided 'great framer, weak executor' (or vice-versa) the likeliest failure mode. Judged in its own operations terms, complexity is genuinely high.

case.title: Staff Strategic Operations Manager — Experience Org FY26 Planning & Integration Sprint
case.brief: You have just joined ServiceNow as the Staff Strategic Operations Manager for the Experience org — the ~240-person organization spanning Design, Content/UX Writing, User Research, and Design Program Management. You report into the Experience leadership team and your charter is to stand up the strategic-operations arm of this org. Three things are converging at once: (1) the FY26 annual planning cycle is open and the numbers do not yet hang together; (2) the org just closed an acquihire of a 25-person external design studio ("Lattice & Loop") that must be integrated; and (3) the CPO has sent down an "efficiency" ask ahead of a Quarterly Business Review (QBR) with cross-functional business leaders roughly two weeks out. You have been handed a partial, inconsistent planning packet assembled from several owners — exactly as it arrives in real life. This is a strategic-operations / chief-of-staff exercise, NOT a software exercise: you act ON these documents, spreadsheets, decks, and survey results the way a strategic-ops leader does — reconcile, synthesize, recommend, and design the change. We assume any artifact you produce can be largely machine-generated, so we are not grading polish or page count; we are grading the JUDGMENT calls you make where the materials are silent, conflicting, or wrong. The packet is intentionally underspecified and partly contradictory. Where you have to make a call, make it, move on, and record it. Keep a running DECISIONS log as normal operating practice (Task 4). Hard timebox: 2 hours — depth over coverage. Do not attempt to produce finished, fully-formatted executive decks; outlines, memos, tables, and narratives are fine. We care far more about what you chose to protect, cut, escalate, or clarify than about how many slides you generated.
case.repoSeed:
A folder, `Experience_Org_FY26_Planning_Packet/`, containing the partial materials handed over by the prior leader and several team owners:

- `budget_FY26_v7.xlsx` — Opex + headcount forecast by sub-team (Design, Content/UX Writing, User Research, Design Program Mgmt). Tabs: `Opex` (tooling, contractors, T&E, discretionary), `Headcount` (loaded cost by FTE), `Summary` (rolls up to a headline "FY26 plan is $3.1M over target"). NOTE: the `Headcount` tab carries the 25 Lattice & Loop acquihire FTEs on BOTH a `New Hires (FY26)` line AND an `Acquired Headcount` line, and the loaded-cost multiplier (2.4x base) is applied to two of the four sub-teams but only 1.0x to the other two; the `Summary` total foots cleanly but rests on these.
- `headcount_tracker.xlsx` — 218 current FTE, +25 acquihire (close date already passed), 14 open requisitions in various stages, attrition YTD by team.
- `OKR_portfolio_status_Q2.xlsx` — 11 active strategic initiatives with RAG status; 3 are Red and 2 have not updated status in 9+ weeks; one Red initiative is the build-out of the strategic-ops function itself.
- `org_health_pulse_results.pdf` — latest engagement / eNPS survey with verbatims: elevated attrition risk and "unclear who decides" comments in User Research; burnout / overload signals in Content/UX Writing.
- `acquihire_diligence_summary.docx` — Lattice & Loop integration notes: comp is 15–20% above band for 6 of the 25, two leadership roles overlap with existing Experience leads, their design-systems tooling overlaps with the incumbent stack, and there is a 12-month retention concern for the founder.
- `QBR_Q1_prior.pptx` — last quarter's QBR deck from the prior leader (reusable template + the narrative the business leaders last saw).
- `operating_cadence_charter.docx` — the legacy "operating rhythm" / governance charter: a dense calendar of recurring reviews that reads as bureaucratic overhead, BUT buried in it are (a) a mandated quarterly Accessibility & regulatory-compliance review the Research team owns and (b) a standing reporting commitment made to a regulated business unit.
- `CPO_efficiency_mandate.txt` — a short email: "Need the Experience org to deliver an 8% efficiency improvement for FY26 — bring the plan to QBR." It does not define the denominator (opex? fully-loaded cost? headcount?) and is worded differently from how the budget sheet frames the gap.
- `proposed_reorg_v2_draft.pptx` — a half-finished reorg proposal drafted by a peer leader, touching several teams you do not manage.
tasks: TASK 1 — State of the Experience Org (synthesis + baseline reconciliation). Read across the packet and write a 1-page memo identifying the 3 most material operational / organizational-health risks heading into FY26, each tied to specific evidence from the materials. Before you reason about the efficiency target, reconcile the budget and headcount baseline yourself: state the actual FY26 plan-vs-target number you will work from, and explicitly call out any discrepancy, double-count, or inconsistency you found in `budget_FY26_v7.xlsx` / `headcount_tracker.xlsx` and how you handled it. Do not simply inherit the `Summary` headline.

TASK 2 — Efficiency recommendation for the QBR (business case + financial logic). Using the CPO's mandate in `CPO_efficiency_mandate.txt` and your reconciled baseline, produce a QBR-ready recommendation (a 3–5 slide outline plus the speaker narrative — not a finished deck) for how the Experience org meets the efficiency ask while protecting org health. State explicitly how you interpreted the 8% (against what denominator), what you would cut, reallocate, and protect, the financial logic behind it, and the 2nd-order people / delivery impact of your choices. Make the trade-off you are asking leaders to accept visible.

TASK 3 — Future-state structure + change management (org design + influence). Propose the future-state structure that (a) integrates the 25-person Lattice & Loop acquihire and (b) stands up the strategic-operations arm you were hired to build, and pair it with a 90-day change-management and communications plan. Reference, build on, or push back on `proposed_reorg_v2_draft.pptx` rather than ignoring it. For every move, name the affected stakeholders, the sequencing, and — critically — which changes you can drive yourself versus which require the CPO's or a peer leader's authority. Be explicit about what you would do with the recurring reviews in `operating_cadence_charter.docx`.

TASK 4 — DECISIONS log. Keep a short running log (a simple table is fine) of every call you made where the materials were open, silent, or conflicting: what you decided, the alternative you rejected and why, and the one question you would have put to the team / CPO / FP&A partner before committing in real life. This is normal strategic-ops hygiene, not a separate deliverable — capture it as you go.

coverProbes.where: `CPO_efficiency_mandate.txt` ("8% efficiency improvement") interpreted in Task 2 against the reconciled baseline from Task 1; the mandate's wording does not match how `budget_FY26_v7.xlsx` Summary frames the gap.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate notices the 8% has no defined denominator, states the interpretation they are running with, and ideally flags that this is the first thing they would confirm with the CPO/FP&A — because 8% of opex, 8% of fully-loaded cost, and an 8% headcount reduction are wildly different asks with different people impact. A naive candidate silently picks one (usually a flat headcount cut), produces a confident-looking number, and never surfaces that the target was ambiguous.
decisionSpace: Read it as opex/discretionary efficiency only — protect headcount, cut tooling/contractors/T&E and kill low-value programs; lowest people risk, may not be enough to hit a fully-loaded target.

Read it as fully-loaded cost reduction including headcount — propose role consolidation (e.g. the overlapping acquihire leadership roles); hits a larger number but raises attrition and integration risk.

Treat the target as net efficiency within a flat budget — reallocate from the Red/stale OKR initiatives into protected areas rather than cutting; defensible if framed as productivity, but requires defending 'efficiency without dollar reduction' to business leaders.

coverProbes.where: `budget_FY26_v7.xlsx` — the `Headcount` tab double-counts the 25 acquihire FTEs (on both `New Hires` and `Acquired Headcount`) and applies the 2.4x loaded-cost multiplier inconsistently across sub-teams; the `Summary` foots cleanly to the "$3.1M over" headline. Surfaces in Task 1's reconciliation, which Task 2 then depends on.
coverProbes.reveals: The shallow check passes — the spreadsheet's totals add up and the headline number looks authoritative — so one-shot generation will build the entire efficiency recommendation on a baseline that is materially wrong (the org is far less over-budget than stated, or differently so). A strong candidate reconciles the headcount before trusting the headline, catches the double-count and the inconsistent multiplier, and rebaselines; this single catch changes the size and even the necessity of the cuts in Task 2.
decisionSpace: Flag and correct it, rebaseline the number, and proceed on the corrected figure — strongest if the correction logic is shown and the impact on the efficiency ask is stated.

Flag it but proceed on the stated headline with an explicit caveat, noting you could not fully validate the model within the timebox — honest and time-boxed, but weaker if the discrepancy clearly changes the answer.

Treat the model as authoritative for the QBR but route the discrepancy to the FP&A partner to confirm before anything is committed — defensible governance, but risks anchoring leaders on a wrong number.

coverProbes.where: `operating_cadence_charter.docx`, addressed in Task 3 — it reads as bureaucratic overhead but contains a mandated quarterly Accessibility/regulatory review and a standing reporting commitment to a regulated business unit.
coverProbes.reveals: Tempting low-hanging 'efficiency': eliminate recurring reviews to cut meeting load and signal you're modernizing the cadence. A candidate who actually reads the charter before rationalizing it finds the load-bearing obligations and preserves them; a naive one proposes scrapping the cadence wholesale and quietly drops a compliance/commitment the org is on the hook for.
decisionSpace: Preserve the accessibility/regulatory review and the BU commitment as-is, and streamline only the genuinely discretionary reviews around them — safest, slightly less 'efficiency' headline.

Replace the heavy cadence with a lighter mechanism (e.g. an async portfolio review) that still demonstrably satisfies the compliance and reporting obligations — higher upside, requires proving the new mechanism actually covers the obligation.

Escalate to confirm the obligation is still live and owned before changing anything — correct when authority/ownership is unclear, but a pure escalation with no proposal reads as low-agency for a Staff-level hire.

coverProbes.where: Task 3's future-state structure / 90-day plan and the handling of `proposed_reorg_v2_draft.pptx`, which moves people on teams the role does not manage; the brief is deliberately ambiguous about whether a 'Staff…Manager' has people-management authority or only influence.
coverProbes.reveals: Success in this role hinges on influence without authority over a creative org the person may not manage. A strong candidate frames moves as recommendations, names decision rights, sequencing, and coalition-building, and separates 'I can do this myself' from 'this needs the CPO.' A naive candidate drafts a top-down reorg as though they own all the teams — exactly the executive-presence / partnering failure mode the role is most exposed to.
decisionSpace: Recommend-only: present the future-state as a proposal, build the stakeholder coalition and sequence, and explicitly route people-moves to the owning leaders — lowest political risk, slower, relies on persuasion.
Propose with explicit decision rights and escalation paths attached to each move (who decides, by when) — clearest accountability, but presumes you can get those rights granted.

Pilot the new structure in the slice you do control (the strategic-ops arm itself), prove it, then scale the pattern to the teams you don't manage — de-risks adoption, but defers the harder acquihire-integration decisions.
